title: Closed doors
hookLine: at a conference by a lake, nations refuse refugees; a ship full of Jewish families is turned away

cards: Where do you go when nobody will let you in? A grand hotel on the shore of a lake in France. Delegates from many countries arrive in good suits.
There are speeches, dinners, walks by the water. They have come to talk about Jews trying to get out of Germany and Austria.
Delegate after delegate stands up, expresses sympathy, and explains why their own country cannot take more. The meeting ends. The visas don't come.

teach.b: The town was Evian, and the year was 1938. The conference there is remembered for what it did not do. Countries spoke of quotas, of jobs, of their own troubles at home.
Very few doors opened. For Jews in Germany and Austria, the problem was no longer only getting out. It was finding anywhere that would let them in.
The next year, a ship called the St.
Louis sailed from Germany carrying Jewish refugees, families who had sold what they could to buy passage and landing papers for Cuba.
When the ship reached Havana, the papers were declared no good, and most of the passengers were not allowed to land.
The ship sailed on, close enough to the coast of the United States to see it, and asked to be let in there. The answer was no. Canada said no too.

Louis turned around and sailed back across the ocean. In the end, several European countries took the passengers in. Some of them were later caught when the war reached those countries, and did not survive.
Closed doors were not only walls and guards.
They were forms, quotas, and polite refusals in good suits.
The Torah has a command that speaks to it: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The command rests on memory: you know what it is to be the one outside.
Jewish tradition keeps returning to the stranger, the person at the door with nowhere else to go. This chapter is part of why.

how: Jewish teaching returns often to the command to love the stranger, and some Jewish refugee organizations today point to this history when they help refugees from anywhere.

games.q: you are on the St. Louis. Havana will not let you land. the ship sails north along the American coast. what happens next?
o: the United States lets the ship dock.
the ship is refused again and sails back to Europe.
the passengers are allowed off in Canada.
games.why: the United States said no, and Canada said no. the ship sailed back across the ocean, and several European countries took the passengers in.

practice: Bring to mind someone on the outside of something right now: a newcomer at work, a neighbor who doesn't know anyone, someone looking for a job, a room, a seat at the table. Stay with them a moment, without fixing anything.
Then let one small opening take shape: an introduction, an invitation, a chair pulled out.

wordCard.voice: Closed doors. The refusals at Evian, the ship turned away from Havana and from North America: the countries that would not let Jewish refugees in. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the stranger, the one who lives among a people not their own. the Torah asks again and again that the ger be loved.

carryVoice: Your line: doors closed. Every refusal had a family standing on the other side of it. See you tomorrow.
